the_gap: SourceAccessBudget.reader_bytes was a declared ceiling that was never consulted inside the governed read path, so it constrained nothing.

design.principle: Enforce the ceiling in the file-like read() the compiled reader already calls, and surface the breach at the OUTER decode boundary where raising is both prompt and loud.
design.why_not_raising_through_the_callback: An exception raised inside a file-like object that a compiled C extension is calling from arbitrary internal state is not a reliable failure channel. Depending on the extension it can be swallowed, converted into a short read, or left to hang. The limiter therefore never raises.
limiter_behaviour: Armed per compiled-reader invocation with the remaining allowance (cap minus reader_bytes already consumed), so it covers reader traffic only; the application's hash and header-prefix reads keep their own separate accounts and caps.
A request larger than the remaining allowance is SHORTENED to exactly the allowance. That is a legitimate partial read, not a breach by itself.
When the allowance reaches zero the limiter returns b"" so the reader observes a clean end of stream and terminates on its own. No exception crosses the bridge.
truncated / exhausted are recorded on the governed open, never raised there.
design.outer_boundary: After the reader returns, or raises, the broker accounts the exact consumed bytes and raises SourceAccessViolation(READER_BYTES_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) if truncated or exhausted.
design.reader_error_conversion: On a truncated stream pyreadstat raises its own ReadstatError('Unable to read from file'). That is captured, accounted exactly, and re-raised as a typed READER_BYTES_LIMIT_EXCEEDED chained from the original, so the refusal is attributable to the byte ceiling rather than looking like a generic reader fault. If the limiter did NOT trip, the original error is re-raised unchanged.

requirements.never_read_a_byte_beyond_the_limit: PROVED — the limiter clamps every request to the remaining allowance, so bytes_read is monotonic and bounded. Measured across ceilings 1, 10, 64, 200, needed-1, needed, needed+1 and needed*4 on a 3-column/60-row carrier: bytes_read <= cap in every case.
requirements.accounting_remains_exact: PROVED — reader_bytes and reader_read_calls are now attributed by DELTA across each reader invocation rather than read as an absolute of the whole open. Previously the account folded the application's hash and header-prefix reads into reader_bytes; that inflation is fixed, and court C11e asserts the two are distinct.
requirements.failure_prompt_and_loud_at_outer_boundar: PROVED — refusal latency measured at ~0.2 ms against a 10 s hang threshold (court C11b), and the message names the ceiling and the exact consumption.
requirements.no_raise_through_pyreadstat_callback: PROVED by construction and asserted by court C11c, which drives the governed view directly under an armed allowance and shows it returns short/empty rather than propagating an exception.
requirements.negative_tests_prove_bytes_never_exceed_: PROVED — C11 (sweep), C11b (promptness), C11c (bridge safety), C11d (partial vs excess), C11e (accounting scope), C11f (decoder boundary).
requirements.distinguish_allowed_partial_final_read_f: PROVED — at a ceiling exactly equal to the required bytes the reader completes and no refusal occurs; one byte short the run is refused having consumed exactly cap bytes. A partial read that still satisfies the reader sets neither truncated nor exhausted and is not a breach.

invariants.accounting_exact_at_refusal: the refusal carries account_snapshot with the exact bytes consumed
invariants.opt_in: reader_bytes defaults to None (unbounded), so the default decode path is unchanged and no existing caller is affected

results.note: exactly enough: reader completes, not a breach
